# Vasala Sutta (Snp 1.7 (PTS Snp 21))
**ID:** Snp 1.7 (PTS Snp 21)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Vasala Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.7
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Vasala Sutta* (Snp 1.7) is the seventh discourse of the Uragavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Sarath-Chandra 2007; Shigaraki & Matsumoto 2013]. Set while the Buddha is on alms-round in Sāvatthī, the text opens with the sacrificial fire-tending brahmin Aggikabhāradvāja abusing the approaching Buddha as a shaveling (*muṇḍaka*) and an outcaste (*vasalaka*) [Chan 2009; Dutt 2004; Silk 2020]. The Buddha calms the brahmin and asks whether he knows what an outcaste is or what actions make one an outcaste [Chan 2009; Silk 2020]. In the subsequent verses, the Buddha thoroughly redefines the category of the outcaste (*vasala*, Sanskrit *vṛṣala*), demonstrating that outcaste status is determined solely by moral and immoral conduct—such as harming living beings, deceit, and anger—rather than by hereditary social birth, culminating in the declaration that one becomes an outcaste or a brahmin by one's deeds [SuttaCentral; Chan 2009; Sweet 1977; Silk 2020]. Verse 137 specifically references the renowned sage Sopāka Mātaṅga to demonstrate that even someone born to an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*) family could attain spiritual heights [Silk 2020].
Full parallels are preserved in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* collections as SA 102 (T 99) and SA2 268 (T 100), where the term *vasala* is transliterated or translated using expressions such as *caṇḍāla* (旃陀羅) and the obscure title *lǐngqúntè* (領群特) [SuttaCentral; Silk 2020]. DharmaNexus detects automated alignments with these Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* texts as well as with Sanskrit texts including the *Kalpadrumāvadānamālā* [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, the sutta is mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Diṭṭhikathā*) [SuttaCentral] and is included in an expanded recension of the *Catubhāṇavārapāḷi* paritta collection [Anālayo 2018]. DharmaNexus also records extensive Pali-internal text reuse (248 matches across 34 texts), sharing substantial verse and prose segments with the *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7), the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), and the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for snp1.7 (Vasalasutta) — Basic metadata, English title, blurb, list of translations, canonical mention in Ps 1.2, and parallels in the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (SA 102, SA2 268).
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel analysis for snp1.7 — Identified text reuse with SN 7, AN 10, the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, and cross-language alignments with T 99 and Kalpadrumāvadānamālā.
- [Sarath-Chandra 2007] Tanuja Yasanga Sarath-Chandra, Buddhism: Answers to 12 Common Questions (2007) — Identifies the placement of the Vasala Sutta within the Uragavagga of the Suttanipāta.
- [Chan 2009] Chan Khoon San, Buddhist Pilgrimage (New Ed., 2009) — Details the setting at Sāvatthī with Aggikabhāradvāja, the definition of an outcaste by deeds rather than birth, and its invocation by B. R. Ambedkar in 1956.
- [Gombrich 1991] Richard F. Gombrich, Buddhist Precept and Practice (1991) — Reports the use of the sutta's anti-caste maxims by modern Amarapura monks in Sri Lanka and notes the commentarial setting.
- [Dutt 2004] Sukumar Dutt, Early Buddhist Monachism (1924) — Notes the fire-sacrifice context of Aggika Bhāradvāja and hostility toward shaven-headed ascetics.
- [Shigaraki & Matsumoto 2013] Takamaro Shigaraki and David Matsumoto, Heart of the Shin Buddhist Path (2013) — Confirms placement in Uragavagga and cites translation by Piyadassi Thera.
- [Anālayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Rebirth in Early Buddhism & Current Research (2018) — Notes the inclusion of the Vasala Sutta in the extended Catubhāṇavārapāḷi collection.
- [Sweet 1977] Michael Jay Sweet, Śāntideva and the Mādhyamika (1977) — Quotes the central dictum of the sutta that deeds, not birth, define a brahmin or outcaste.
- [Silk 2020] Jonathan A. Silk, Indian Buddhist Attitudes toward Outcastes: Rhetoric around Caṇḍālas — Analyzes the terminology vasala/vṛṣala, the Chinese parallel in T 99, the Buddha's redefinition of vasala, and the reference to Sopāka Mātaṅga in verse 137.
- [Saddhatissa 2013] H. Saddhatissa, The Sutta-Nipāta: A New Translation from the Pali Canon (2013) — Lists early English translations of the Vasala Sutta by Ananda Metteyya and Nārada Mahāthera.
